content.title: Merge Conflicts: When Two Histories Touch the Same Lines
content.hook: Two engineers start from a similar version of a file.
content.context:
Engineer A changes:

```js
const heading = "Dashboard";
```

to:

```js
const heading = "Account Dashboard";
```

Engineer B changes the same line to:

```js
const heading = "Overview";
```

Now Git cannot safely guess which final line the team wants.

That is a merge conflict.
goals: Understand why merge conflicts happen and resolve a simple conflict by comparing the competing versions rather than choosing blindly.

content.title: Conflict markers
content.text:
A simplified conflicted file might look like:

```text
<<<<<<< HEAD
const heading = "Account Dashboard";
=======
const heading = "Overview";
>>>>>>> feature/overview-title
```

Do not panic when you see this.

The file is showing you that two versions disagree.

content.question: What should you ask before deleting the conflict markers?

options.text: “What behavior should the final code have?”

feedback.correct: Conflict resolution is an engineering decision, not a contest between authors.
feedback.incorrect: Conflict resolution is an engineering decision, not a contest between authors.

content.title: Resolve by intent
content.text:
Suppose the product requirement says:

> “The dashboard should use the title Account Dashboard.”

Then the final code should be:

```js
const heading = "Account Dashboard";
```

The conflict markers disappear because you have selected the intended final state.

content.title: Conflicts can be larger
content.text:
Sometimes both engineers change different parts of a file and Git can combine them automatically.

Sometimes the changes overlap in a way Git cannot safely combine.

The rule stays the same:

**Read both sides, understand the intended final behavior, then produce one correct final version.**

content.question:
A conflict appears in a file.

What does it mean?

options.text: Git found competing changes that require a human decision.
The code cannot be edited again.

feedback.correct: A conflict is a prompt for engineering judgment.
feedback.incorrect: A conflict is a prompt for engineering judgment.

activities.title: Checkpoint
activities.instruction: Arrange the steps in the most logical sequence.

content.prompt: List the steps in the safest order:

feedback.correct: Decide what the code should mean before editing the markers away.
feedback.incorrect: Decide what the code should mean before editing the markers away.

content.title: Forge takeaway & Lesson completion
takeaways: **Mental model:** A merge conflict is not a Git failure. It is an unresolved design decision between two versions of history.
**Senior habit:** Resolve the behavior first. Edit the conflict markers second.
nextSteps: Explain why blindly choosing “ours” or “theirs” can produce a technically resolved but behaviorally wrong merge.
